## {#today .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.todaymeta}
Session 2 of day 3, on the models of a yes-or-no outcome
:::

:::: {.todaybox}
::: {.nonincremental .fs-85}
1. Proportions – a 0/1 outcome, its share, and the difference between two shares
2. The linear probability model – the difference as a regression, with HC2 standard errors
3. Logistic regression – log odds, odds ratios against average marginal effects, and what a covariate does to an odds ratio
:::
::::

::: {.todaytake .fs-85}
You leave able to say what each model of the menu estimates, on which scale it reports, and why the course reports every model in percentage points
:::

::: {.todaymeta}
Work along in the workspace, in your IDE (Positron, RStudio, VS Code, etc.)
:::

::: notes
The second session takes the outcome of the claim as its subject: whether a reply opened with the name of the sender, a yes or a no. Yesterday the menu offered two models for it, a difference in proportions and a logistic regression, and you chose between them in Task 4 and again in your declaration. This session explains what each model does. We start from a table of four counts and the difference between two shares, then write the same difference as a linear regression and give it the standard errors that the course uses throughout. Then the logistic regression of the paper, which reports odds ratios, and the reason why the course turns every logit into percentage points, which has to do with what a covariate does to an odds ratio, even in an experiment.
:::

# PART 1 – Proportions {#part-1-proportions .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 1
:::

::: notes
Part one starts where every analysis of this claim starts, with four counts: the replies to each group of names, and how many of them opened with the name of the sender. The reference specification of the curve uses nothing else, and three of the five analysts worked from a table of four counts of the same kind. Everything else in this session is a way of describing the difference between two shares, and of saying how far it could have arisen by chance, so it pays to be clear about the share itself first.
:::

## A 0/1 outcome {#a-binary-outcome .smaller}

::: {.fs-80}
| Names | Coded replies | Greeted by name | Share | Variance $p(1 - p)$ |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|--:|
| White | 175 | 107 | 61.1% | 0.238 |
| Hispanic | 187 | 77 | 41.2% | 0.242 |
:::

::: {.small}
- A reply either opened with the name of the sender or it did not: the outcome takes the values 1 and 0, and **its mean in a group is the share** greeted by name
- **Its variance follows from the share**, $p(1 - p)$, largest at one half, so two groups whose shares differ also differ in their variance
- Every model of this session describes the probability of a 1, and how it differs between the two groups of names
:::

::: {.src}
The rows of the reference specification: the coded replies to Hispanic and white names in cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv.
:::

::: notes
Here are the four counts: of the hundred and seventy-five coded replies to white names, a hundred and seven opened with the name of the sender, and of the hundred and eighty-seven to Hispanic names, seventy-seven did. Code a greeting by name as one and anything else as zero, and the mean of that variable in a group is simply the share. That is why everything in this session can be read as a statement about a share, or a probability. The last column matters for what follows. The variance of a zero-or-one variable is fixed by its share, p times one minus p, which is largest at one half. Here the two shares sit on either side of one half, so their variances are almost the same, but in general two groups whose shares differ also differ in how variable their outcome is.
:::

## The difference in proportions {#the-difference-in-proportions .smaller}

::: {.small}
- The difference: **−19.97 percentage points**, the scale on which the abstract states the claim
- Its standard error combines the two group variances: **5.16** points, and a 95% confidence interval from −30.1 to −9.8
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
- The classical test of the same table: $\chi^2$ = **14.42**, the square of the *z* of a test of two proportions with a pooled share
- With the continuity correction of Yates, which shrinks each gap between an observed and an expected count by half a unit before squaring: $\chi^2$ = **13.63**. `chisq.test()` and `prop.test()` apply it to every two by two table unless told otherwise
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
In Task 3 the value recorded for 8PTRZ, $\chi^2$ = 14.265, was the corrected one: uncorrected, 14.952. A table carries no covariates, so the curve tests every specification by its model instead.
:::

::: {.src}
cases/housing/data/spec_curve.csv (the reference specification) and display_outcomes.csv; the table of 8PTRZ from audit_original.csv.
:::

::: notes
The plainest summary is the difference between the two shares, minus twenty points, which is also the scale of the claim in the abstract. Its standard error follows from the two variances of the last slide, each divided by the size of its group, and gives an interval from minus thirty to minus ten. [advance] The classical test of a table is the chi-square, and without a correction it is exactly the square of the z of a test of two proportions. Chisq dot test and prop dot test apply the continuity correction of Yates to any two-by-two table unless you tell them not to: each difference between an observed and an expected count shrinks by half a unit before it is squared, which makes the test a little more conservative. [advance] You met this in Task 3. The value on record for 8PTRZ is the corrected one: nobody asked for the correction, and the default of the function supplied it.
:::

# PART 2 – The linear probability model {#part-2-the-linear-probability-model .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 2
:::

::: notes
Part two writes the same difference as a regression. That sounds like a detour, but it is what lets the analysis carry covariates, and it is the model of the reference specification of the curve, the one that most of you met first in Task 4. We look at what its two coefficients are, at its one well-known fault, and then at its standard errors, because the classical formula makes an assumption that a zero-or-one outcome breaks.
:::

## The linear probability model {#the-linear-probability-model .smaller}

```{.r}
lpm <- lm(y ~ hisp, data = frame)                     # frame <- spec_frame(audit)
parameters::model_parameters(lpm, vcov = "HC2")
```

::: {.small}
- A linear regression of the 0/1 outcome on the 0/1 indicator of the Hispanic names: the intercept, **0.611**, is the share for the white names, and the coefficient, **−0.200**, is the difference in proportions
- A straight line has no floor or ceiling, so with covariates it **can predict shares below 0 or above 1**. With the covariates of the curve, its predictions here run from 0.21 to 0.79
- In an experiment its coefficient estimates the difference in proportions, the quantity that the claim names, with or without covariates. That is why the reference specification of the curve is this model, without covariates
:::

::: notes
A linear regression of the greeting, zero or one, on an indicator that is one for the Hispanic names is called a linear probability model. With a single binary predictor it reproduces the table exactly. Its intercept is the share for the white names, sixty-one per cent, and its coefficient is the difference, minus twenty points, so the model reports in the units of the claim from the start. Its well-known fault appears once covariates enter. A straight line has no floor or ceiling, so it can predict a share below zero or above one. With the handful of categories that the curve uses as covariates, its predictions here stay well inside that range. And in an experiment its coefficient keeps estimating the quantity that the claim names, with covariates or without, which is why the reference specification is this model.
:::

## HC2 standard errors {#hc2-standard-errors .smaller}

::: {.small}
- **Classical** errors assume that the outcome varies equally in every group, which a 0/1 outcome cannot do when the shares differ
- **HC2** errors, one of the heteroskedasticity-consistent or 'robust' errors, let each observation keep its own variance. With one binary predictor they equal the standard error computed group by group, the formula for two randomised groups
:::

::: {.fs-80}
| Standard error of the gap | Points |
|:--|--:|
| Classical, from `lm()` | 5.167 |
| HC2, from `parameters::model_parameters(lpm, vcov = "HC2")` | 5.165 |
| Group by group, from `t.test()` | 5.165 |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
The groups are similar in size and in share, so the classical error is close. When groups differ both in size and in variance, or covariates enter, the two part, and HC2 is the one that stays right, which is why the curve uses it throughout.
:::

::: {.src}
The reference specification on cases/housing/data/housing_audit.csv; HC2 errors from sandwich through parameters, as in the estimator of the course (R/housing/_tools.R).
:::

::: notes
Now the standard errors, because the menu fixes them and the estimator of the course uses one kind throughout. The classical formula of a linear regression assumes one common variance for every observation. A zero-or-one outcome breaks that whenever the shares differ, because its variance is fixed by its share. HC2 errors, one member of the family that people call robust errors, let each observation keep its own variance, and with one binary predictor they come out exactly as the standard error that you would compute group by group, the textbook formula for two randomised groups. [advance] On our data the classical error is close, because the two groups are similar in size and in share. When groups differ both in size and in variance, or when covariates enter, the two can part, and the HC2 error is the one that stays right.
:::

## Hands-on 1 – The table and the linear model {#hands-on-1-the-table-and-the-linear-model .smaller}

::: {.small}
**In the workspace**, with the setup chunk of `index.qmd` run:

1. `frame <- spec_frame(audit)` gives the rows of the reference specification, with the outcome `y` and the indicator `hisp`
2. The table and its tests: `counts <- table(frame$hisp, frame$y)`, then `chisq.test(counts)` and `chisq.test(counts, correct = FALSE)`. **Which one is the square of a z?**
3. The model: `lpm <- lm(y ~ hisp, data = frame)`, then `parameters::model_parameters(lpm)` and `parameters::model_parameters(lpm, vcov = "HC2")`
4. Check two equalities: the coefficient against the difference of the two shares, and the HC2 error against `t.test(y ~ hisp, data = frame)$stderr`
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
Then change one thing: `frame <- spec_frame(audit, comparison = "nonhispanic")`, Hispanic names against white and Black names together, and run steps 3 and 4 again.
:::

::: notes
Your turn. Spec underscore frame, one of the helpers of the workspace, gives you the rows of any specification of the curve, and with no arguments the reference: the coded replies to Hispanic and white names, with the outcome as y and the Hispanic names coded one in hisp. Make the table, then run the chi-square test with the correction and without it, and decide which of the two is the square of a z. Then fit the linear probability model and print its parameters twice, once with the classical errors and once with HC2. Check that the coefficient is the difference between the two shares, and that the HC2 error equals the standard error that t dot test computes group by group. [state the time] [advance] Then compare with white and Black names together, where the groups are of unequal size, and see whether the two errors part. They barely do, because the two shares give almost the same variance, and that is worth a sentence in your notes.
:::

# PART 3 – Logistic regression {#part-3-logistic-regression .darkslide background-color="rgba(0,0,0,0)"}

::: {.partlabel}
Part 3
:::

::: notes
Part three turns to the model of the paper. The original authors, the OAs, fitted a logistic regression, and so did three of the five analysts, so this is the model behind the published result and behind two of the four statistics that Multi100 recorded for the analysts. A logistic regression does not report in percentage points. It reports differences in log odds, and their exponents, odds ratios. We look at what that scale is, how to get back to the scale of the claim, and why the course does so for every logit on the curve.
:::

## Logistic regression {#logistic-regression .smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](housing-binary-outcomes_files/figure-revealjs/d3-logistic-curve-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.small}
- The model describes the **log odds** of a greeting, $\log(p / (1 - p))$, which run over the whole real line, so every prediction stays between 0 and 1
- The coefficient of the Hispanic names is **−0.810**, with *z* = −3.771, the value recorded for UYV3F. Its exponent is the **odds ratio**, 0.445
- Without covariates the model reproduces the two shares exactly, so its gap in points is the same −19.97. The paper reports −0.82 from three groups with covariates
:::

::: {.src}
The coefficient of the paper: @EinsteinGlick2017DoesRaceAffect, Table 1, model 3. Logistic regression read on the scale of probabilities: @GelmanEtAl2020RegressionOtherStories.
:::

::: notes
The logistic regression works on the log odds of a greeting, the log of the share divided by one minus the share. Log odds run from minus infinity to plus infinity, so a straight line on that scale never predicts an impossible share, and the curve on the slide takes it back to probabilities. The two points are our two groups of names. The coefficient of the Hispanic names, minus point eight one, is the horizontal step between them, a difference in log odds, and its z is exactly the value that Multi100 recorded for UYV3F. Exponentiated, it is an odds ratio of about point four four. The vertical step is the gap in points, minus twenty. Without covariates the logit reproduces the two observed shares exactly, so here the two scales tell the same story. The minus point eight two of the paper comes from a model with all three groups and with covariates.
:::

## From odds ratios to percentage points {#from-odds-ratios-to-percentage-points .smaller}


::: {.cell}
::: {.cell-output-display}
![](housing-binary-outcomes_files/figure-revealjs/d3-or-gaps-1.png){width=912}
:::
:::


::: {.small}
- One odds ratio means very different gaps at different shares: −10.0 points at a share of 20% for the white names, −20.0 at the 61% of the data, −10.0 at 90%
- The **average marginal effect** predicts every email as if it carried a Hispanic name and as if it carried a white one, and averages the difference: −19.97 points here (SE 5.15), from `marginaleffects::avg_comparisons()` [@Arel-BundockEtAl2024HowInterpretStatistical]
- Across the 32 logits of the curve, the odds ratio runs from 0.443 to 0.533 and the average marginal effect from −20.0 to −12.2 points
:::

::: notes
Odds ratios are exact and portable, but they are hard to picture, because one odds ratio means very different changes in probability at different starting points. The curve applies the odds ratio of our data to every possible share of greetings for the white names. At the sixty-one per cent of the data it gives the gap of twenty points. At twenty per cent, or at ninety, the same odds ratio gives a gap of only ten. So an odds ratio on its own does not say how large the gap is in points. The average marginal effect does: predict every email as if it carried a Hispanic name, then as if it carried a white one, and average the difference. That puts any logit back on the scale of the claim. A rule of thumb follows from the same curve: a logistic coefficient moves a probability by at most a quarter of its value, so the coefficient of nought point nought nine eight found by the replication is at most two and a half points.
:::

## Odds ratios and covariates {#odds-ratios-and-covariates .smaller}

::: {.small}
In an experiment, a covariate that predicts the outcome leaves the target of a difference in proportions unchanged, but it changes the target of an odds ratio, with no confounding at all. The odds ratio is **non-collapsible**: two kinds of authority, equally many of each, and the odds ratio of the data within each kind:
:::

::: {.fs-80}
| | Kind A | Kind B | All authorities |
|:--|--:|--:|--:|
| White names greeted by name | 85.0% | 35.0% | 60.0% |
| Hispanic names greeted by name | 71.6% | 19.3% | 45.5% |
| Gap (points) | −13.4 | −15.7 | −14.5 |
| Odds ratio | 0.445 | 0.445 | 0.556 |
:::

::: {.fragment .small}
On the data, the hard-to-find address predicts the greeting, which opened 65.7% of the replies to white names from easy addresses and 53.7% of those from hard ones, and chance spread it almost evenly across the two groups of names. Adding it moves the logit coefficient from −0.810 to −0.814, away from zero, and leaves the gap at −19.95 points.
:::

::: notes
Here is the least familiar property of the odds ratio. In an experiment, adding a covariate that predicts the outcome does not change what a difference in proportions estimates, because the covariate is unrelated to the name. It does change what an odds ratio estimates, even though nothing is confounded. Imagine two kinds of authority, equally many of each, where white names are greeted by name eighty-five and thirty-five per cent of the time, and let the Hispanic names have the odds ratio of our data in both. Within each kind, the odds ratio is point four four. For all authorities together it is point five six, closer to one, while the gap in points for all is the average of the two gaps. [advance] On our data the effect is small: the address predicts the greeting moderately and fell evenly on the names, so the coefficient moves a little away from zero and the gap does not move. Two odds ratios from different models answer different questions, which is why the course reports every logit in points.
:::

## Hands-on 2 – The logit and its two scales {#hands-on-2-the-logit-and-its-two-scales .smaller}

::: {.small}
**In the workspace**, with `frame` from Hands-on 1 back at the reference, `spec_frame(audit)`:

1. `cols <- datawizard::data_select(frame, c("y", "hisp", "hard_email"))`, because marginaleffects refuses a data column called `group`
2. `logit <- glm(y ~ hisp, family = binomial(), data = cols)`, then `parameters::model_parameters(logit, exponentiate = TRUE)` for the odds ratio
3. `marginaleffects::avg_predictions(logit, variables = list(hisp = 0:1))` for the two average predictions, and `marginaleffects::avg_comparisons(logit, variables = "hisp")` for their difference
4. Add the address, `glm(y ~ hisp + hard_email, ...)`, and run steps 2 and 3 again. **Which of the two scales moves?**
:::

::: notes
Your turn again, with the reference rows from the first hands-on. One detail of marginaleffects catches people out: it refuses a data column called group, and the rows from spec underscore frame carry one, so keep only the columns of the model before you fit. Fit the logit, and print its parameters with exponentiate set to true, which turns the coefficient into an odds ratio. Then ask marginaleffects for the two average predictions, every email as a white name and every email as a Hispanic name, and for their difference, the average marginal effect. Then add the hard-to-find address and repeat. Write down which of the two scales moved and which stayed put, and in one sentence why. [state the time] STUCK in chat if you need me.
:::

## The reading and the next session {#the-reading-and-the-next-session .smaller}

::: {.small .nonincremental}
- **The reading**: [Binary outcomes](../companion/binary-outcomes.html), the module of the companion curriculum behind this session, which builds every model from the table of counts with its code, and sets the methods side by side in one table
- **Next**: Bayesian estimation. The same logistic model fitted to the four counts with priors, the gap of the claim as a posterior distribution, the replication as new data that revise the original estimate, and the errors of sign and of magnitude that a small study risks
:::

::: notes
That is the outcome and its models. The module Binary outcomes is the reading for this session. It builds each model from the table of counts, with the code beside every step, and it ends with a table that sets all the methods side by side on the one comparison of the reference specification, which is worth keeping for your own work. The next session fits the same logistic model again, to the same four counts, but by Bayesian methods. The gap then becomes a distribution about which we can make direct probability statements, and the replication can enter as new data that revise what the original audit told us.
:::
